opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, because the honest answer is that mathematics has always been bottlenecked by human bandwidth. There are only so many people in the world who can work at the research frontier of, say, arithmetic geometry or combinatorics, and each of them has maybe a few decades of productive life. So there are huge regions of the mathematical landscape that nobody has ever walked through. Not because they're uninteresting, but because nobody had the time.

What an AI mathematician can do is change the economics of exploration. If you have a system that can propose conjectures, attempt proofs, and, crucially, verify them formally in something like Lean, then you're not just speeding up one mathematician. You're running thousands of parallel explorations and keeping only what's actually correct. Verification is the key piece for me. In math, unlike a lot of other domains, you can know for certain whether something is right. That gives you a clean signal to build on, and it means the AI's output isn't just plausible-sounding text. It's a checked artifact that a human can trust and extend.

I see a few layers to how this expands discovery. The first is the obvious one: closing open problems, the long tail of lemmas and conjectures that are tedious but tractable. The second, which I find more exciting, is connecting fields. Some of the most beautiful moments in math history come from someone noticing that two distant areas are secretly talking about the same structure. Humans specialize so deeply that those bridges are rare. A system that has, in some sense, read and formalized everything could notice those correspondences far more often.

The third layer is that it changes what questions we even think to ask. When computers first came into number theory, people started seeing patterns in data that led to conjectures like Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer. I think AI mathematicians could be that, but much bigger: a new kind of instrument, like the telescope was for astronomy.

And I don't see this as replacing mathematicians. I see it as giving every mathematician a very tireless, very rigorous collaborator, so the human can focus on taste: deciding what's beautiful, what's important, what's worth pursuing. That part, I think, stays deeply human for a long time.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI exploring mathematics in parallel, but does not say it could reproduce rare geniuses such as Galois or Ramanujan.

r002.rationale: It says AI could change the economics of exploration, but does not apply Jevons paradox or say cheaper mathematical capability would increase its use.

r003.rationale: The response discusses mathematical discovery and connections between fields, but does not suggest scientists collaborating with AI mathematicians could discover scientific theories.

r004.rationale: It compares AI mathematicians to a telescope as an instrument for discovery, but does not identify advances in mathematical tools as enabling major technological transformations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, and that's part of what makes it exciting.

Let me start with how I think about mathematics. Math is this enormous space of possible truths, and human mathematicians have explored only a tiny corner of it. Not because we lack talent, but because of constraints that have nothing to do with intelligence. There are maybe a few tens of thousands of research mathematicians in the world. Each one has a finite career, maybe forty productive years. And each one can hold only so much in their head at once. A number theorist and an algebraic topologist might be working on problems that are secretly the same problem, and neither will ever find out, because no single person can read both literatures deeply.

So the first thing AI mathematicians change is throughput and breadth. If you can have systems that read everything, that can hold the whole literature in view, you start finding those bridges. The history of math is full of moments where a connection between two distant fields unlocked everything. Think of how algebra and geometry got unified, or how the Langlands program ties together number theory and representation theory. Those connections are rare partly because the people who could see them are rare. I think AI can make them much less rare.

The second thing is the scale of exploration. A lot of mathematical discovery is actually search. You try a construction, it fails, you try another one. Human mathematicians develop taste so they don't have to try everything, and that taste is precious. But there are vast regions of the problem space where nobody has good taste yet because nobody has been there. Machines can go there. They can try a million constructions and surface the ones that are interesting. We're already seeing this in combinatorics and in finding counterexamples, where systems produce objects no human would have thought to write down.

The third thing, and this is the one I care most about, is verification. For me, the shift to formal mathematics, where every proof is checked by a machine, is what makes all of this trustworthy. If an AI tells you it proved something and you have to spend six months checking it by hand, you haven't really gained much. But if the proof comes with a formal certificate, then you can trust results you didn't personally verify. That changes the social structure of mathematics. Right now, mathematics runs on trust in individual experts. Formal verification lets it run on something closer to shared infrastructure. And once you have that, you can build much taller. You can stack results on results without the whole thing becoming fragile.

Now, I want to be careful here. I don't think of this as replacing mathematicians. The question that matters most in math is not "can you prove this" but "what is worth proving." That question of what is beautiful, what is deep, what will matter in fifty years, that's a human question, at least for now. What I hope AI does is take care of the parts that are tedious, the checking, the grinding through cases, the literature search, so that humans can spend more time on the parts that require judgment and imagination.

If I think about where this goes in ten or twenty years, I imagine a mathematician sitting down with a system that already knows the entire literature, that can test conjectures in real time, that can tell you "this lemma you just wrote down is actually a special case of a result from 1973 in a field you've never heard of." That mathematician can explore in an afternoon what used to take a career. And collectively, the field can map parts of mathematical reality that would otherwise have stayed dark forever.

So to answer your question directly: I think AI mathematicians expand what humanity can discover by removing the bottlenecks of lifespan, memory, and labor, and by making knowledge cumulative in a way it has never quite been. The truths were always out there. We just couldn't reach them.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI expanding search and connecting mathematical fields, but does not say it could reproduce the capabilities of rare geniuses such as Galois or Ramanujan.

r002.rationale: It discusses removing bottlenecks and expanding exploration, but does not apply the Jevons paradox or say greater accessibility would increase use of mathematical capability.

r003.rationale: The response focuses on mathematical discovery and human mathematicians; it does not describe scientists collaborating with AI mathematicians to discover scientific theories.

r004.rationale: It says mathematical connections have unlocked advances and formal verification could make results cumulative, but does not identify advances in mathematical tools as enabling major technological transformations.

astra-6.text:
I think the most exciting possibility is that AI could expand not just how quickly we solve mathematical problems, but which problems we’re able to tackle at all.

A mathematician has limited time to explore examples, test conjectures, and learn techniques from other fields. An AI collaborator could help explore many more possibilities, find counterexamples, or suggest that a problem has a useful connection to a seemingly unrelated area. The human can then ask: Why does that connection exist? What deeper structure is it pointing to?

But there’s a big difference between producing a proof and producing understanding. Ideally, an AI mathematician would help us do both: establish that something is true and explain it in a way that gives us new concepts and new questions.

So I’d hope the result is more people being able to participate in discovery, and humanity reaching mathematical ideas that would otherwise remain beyond our attention or imagination.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as a mathematical collaborator but does not say it could reproduce the abilities of rare geniuses such as Galois or Ramanujan.

r002.rationale: It hopes more people can participate in discovery, but does not apply the Jevons paradox or say accessibility would increase the use of mathematical capability.

r003.rationale: The response discusses mathematical discovery, not scientists using AI mathematicians to discover new scientific theories.

r004.rationale: It does not identify mathematical tools as enabling major technological transformations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most exciting possibility is that AI could help us discover mathematics we wouldn’t have thought to look for. It could explore examples, notice patterns, and suggest connections between areas that seem unrelated. Those suggestions might give a human mathematician a new question to ask, not just a faster way to answer an existing one.

There’s also a difference between finding a proof and helping us understand why something is true. Ideally, an AI mathematician would do both: produce arguments we can rigorously check, and help us extract the ideas that make those arguments useful elsewhere.

If we get that right, we could expand both the scale of problems we can tackle and the number of people who can participate. Someone with a good intuition but less specialized training could have a collaborator that helps them turn that intuition into a precise conjecture. That could change where discoveries come from.

r002.rationale: It says AI could let more people participate, but does not invoke the Jevons paradox or say increased accessibility would increase use.

r003.rationale: It discusses new mathematical questions and discoveries, but does not suggest scientists working with AI could discover new scientific theories.
